picks.excerpt: Chris Reid argues that humans will stop being the primary readers of published content, and that decades of structured-metadata work (FAIR principles) accidentally prepared publishers for machine readers. A direct challenge to how books and articles should be authored, structured and designed when the audience is an agent.
picks.rationale: Freshest item in the pool and the one that changes practice fastest: if the primary reader is an agent, authoring and structuring decisions move upstream — and it argues publishers already own the metadata groundwork.

picks.excerpt: John Bond and Joanna Penn walk through where generative AI is actually used across publishing operations — including a book that ships AI-generated chapter summaries with usage guidelines — and Bond's claim that mainstream publishers experiment far more than they admit.
picks.rationale: Operational rather than opinion: a named example of AI-generated chapter summaries shipped with disclosure guidelines gives publishers a concrete pattern to copy, plus a read on how much quiet experimentation is already happening.

picks.excerpt: Friedman's industry roundup: EU transparency rules pushing embedded watermarks and signed provenance metadata into future models, a record five journalism award winners disclosing AI use, and HarperCollins' CEO calling for industry-wide AI solutions.
picks.rationale: Tracks the disclosure norm hardening on two fronts at once — award juries accepting declared AI use, and a Big Five CEO asking for industry-wide rules — which is where author and publisher contracts head next.

picks.excerpt: Frankfurt Rights explains why AI licensing requests still have to be negotiated one by one — use, scope, remuneration, reporting and liability differ too much for a standardized workflow — and says the platform has hardened security after sustained attacks from AI bots scraping rights listings.
picks.rationale: The most concrete look yet at how AI licensing actually gets done at the rights desk — five deal terms that resist standardization — plus a genuinely new operational detail: rights platforms are now being scraped by AI bots and are locking down.

picks.excerpt: Dr Alan Finkel, Australia's former chief scientist and founder of Proudly Human, warns that AI delivers "no economic benefits for the arts or the creative sector" and pushes for stronger structural protections for creators against AI-generated content.
picks.rationale: A national-level science figure, not an author-advocate, putting the economic case against AI in the creative sector — the sharpest counterweight in the pool to the adoption-first framing of the other four cards.
